[students] Session 2 - Git Fundamentals & Project Kickoff

1. What we need before starting

You need:

  • Git
  • A GitHub account
  • GitHub CLI (gh)
  • Python 3
  • A terminal
  • A text/code editor, preferably VS Code

These are different tools:

Git             → version control
GitHub          → website/service hosting our remote repositories
GitHub CLI gh   → lets us interact with GitHub from the terminal
Python          → runs our example program
Terminal        → where we type commands
VS Code         → where we edit files

Important: Git and GitHub are not the same thing. Git works locally on your computer.
GitHub is a service that can host a Git repository remotely.

The Git chapters of the textbook only require the Git program. Python is useful in this session because we use a tiny runnable Python project as the starting point. The textbook assumes you already know basic Python.

macOS

What is gh?

Do not confuse:

git

with:

5. Authenticate GitHub CLI

Installing gh is not the same as logging into GitHub.

Run:

gh auth login

When asked, choose:

Where do you use GitHub?
→ GitHub.com

Preferred protocol for Git operations?
→ HTTPS

Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?
→ Yes

How would you like to authenticate GitHub CLI?
→ Login with a web browser

Now you will see something like:

! One-time code (**XXXX-XXXX**) copied to clipboard

**Press Enter** to open https://github.com/login/device in your browser...

Press Enter, a browser will open. Sign into your GitHub account using the XXXX-XXXX code and approve the authentication.

Then verify:

gh auth status

You should see that you are logged into github.com.

Why do we do this?

Git works locally, but eventually we want to send our commits to GitHub.

Authentication tells GitHub:

"This computer is authorised to work with my GitHub account."

The textbook recommends authenticating once per machine with gh auth login, using GitHub.com, HTTPS and browser authentication.

Once you understand these commands, using a graphical interface is perfectly reasonable.

11. What are we learning today?

The session focuses on:

  • why version control matters;
  • creating a local Git repository;
  • staging changes;
  • writing meaningful commit messages;
  • pushing to GitHub;
  • committing after every meaningful change;
  • turning the Session 1 project idea into an initial project;
  • creating the first commit.

The session deliverable is:

Initialized GitHub repository and first runnable commit.

Do not build the complete AI project in this session.

The goal is to establish a real, working starting point.

12. Why version control?

Imagine this:

Your project works.

You change the prompt or code.

You save.

The project stops working.

You want the previous version back.

Without version control, you may have only:

report_final.py
report_final_v2.py
report_final_REAL.py
report_final_FINAL.py

and your memory.

Git solves this by recording project history.

The three jobs of version control

A version control system allows you to:

1. Restore

Return to a previous state of the project.

2. Compare

See what changed between two states.

3. Reconcile

Combine changes made in parallel by different people.

These three functions are central to the textbook's definition of version control.

Definition 1. Version control

A version control system keeps the complete history of a project as an ordered series of recorded states. From that history it can, at any time: restore any past state exactly, show what changed between two states, and reconcile changes made in parallel by different people.

13. Why is version control important for AI and data work?

AI projects are particularly iterative.

You may change:

  • Python code;
  • prompts;
  • model settings;
  • data;
  • configuration;
  • evaluation methods.

A result should be reproducible.

A result you cannot regenerate is a result you cannot trust or defend.

Version control helps connect a project's evolution to concrete recorded states.

For the course project, GitHub should not simply contain the final project at the end. The repository should tell the story of how the project evolved.

14. Core Git vocabulary

Repository

A repository, or repo, is a project folder together with its recorded Git history.

Conceptually:

project folder
+
Git history
=
repository

Commit

A commit is a recorded state of the project.

Think of it as a labelled snapshot.

Important:

A commit is a snapshot of the project, not simply a saved copy of one file.

History

The history is the sequence of commits.

For example:

Commit 1
   ↓
Commit 2
   ↓
Commit 3
   ↓
Commit 4

This creates a record of how the project changed.

15. Git vs GitHub

This distinction must be clear.

Git
│
├── version-control system
├── works locally
├── records commits
└── maintains history

GitHub
│
├── online service
├── hosts Git repositories
├── allows sharing and collaboration
└── provides features such as Pull Requests

Therefore:

git init

does not create a GitHub repository, it turns a plain folder into a Git repository.

And:

git commit

does not upload your work to GitHub. It creates a recorded state of your project directly on your computer (it "takes a picture").

And:

git push

does not create a commit. It takes the commits you have already recorded locally and sends them to a remote repository, such as GitHub.

The core principle to remember is: a commit records locally, while a push shares to the remote repository.

A useful phrase to remember:

Commit records. Push shares.

16. The three important Git states

A change can exist in three relevant places:

Working directory
       │
       │ git add
       ▼
Staging area
       │
       │ git commit
       ▼
Repository / history

Working directory

The files you currently have on your computer. It's also called working tree.

Staging area

The changes selected for the next commit. The staging area is also called the index.

git add selects your changes and puts them into the staging area. It signals to Git that you want to include these specific updates in your next commit.

Repository / history

The changes that have already been recorded as commits (the "album of pictures").

git push creates a recorded snapshot of your project locally. It saves the current state of your staged files directly to your computer's Git history.

17. git status

git status tells you where you are.

Run:

git status

You should develop the habit of using this command frequently.

It can tell you:

  • which branch you are on;
  • whether you have commits;
  • which files are untracked;
  • which files have changed;
  • which changes are staged;
  • whether your working tree is clean.

Now let's work with an easy example, we are going to build Ada together. Ada a small document question-answering assistant: you give it a document and a question, and it answers using only what the document says.

18. Create your first local repository

Choose a location such as your Desktop.

macOS/Linux

cd ~/Desktop
mkdir ada-session2-demo
cd ada-session2-demo

Windows PowerShell

For example:

cd $HOME\Desktop
mkdir ada-session2-demo
cd ada-session2-demo

Check where you are:

pwd

Windows PowerShell:

Get-Location

19. Initialise Git

Run:

git init -b main

This turns the ordinary project folder into a Git repository.

You should see a message similar to:

Initialized empty Git repository in .../ada-session2-demo/.git/

Now run:

git status

You should see something similar to:

On branch main

No commits yet

What just happened?

Git created its internal repository information in:

.git/

Your project is now under Git version control.

But:

  • there are no commits yet;
  • nothing has been pushed;
  • GitHub has not been involved yet.

20. Configure your Git identity

Git records who created each commit.

Configure your name:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"

Configure your email:

git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"

Check:

git config --global user.name
git config --global user.email

When you use git push to send your local history to GitHub, GitHub reads the email address attached to those commits. If the email you configured using git config --global user.email matches the verified email address of your GitHub account, GitHub automatically links those commits to your profile.

This is how GitHub knows to display your avatar, link to your username, and credit you for the work on the repository's history page. If the emails do not match, the commit will still be uploaded, but GitHub will not associate it directly with your account.

You normally do this once per machine.

21. Create a tiny runnable project

For the classroom demonstration, create:

ada-session2-demo/
├── README.md
└── main.py

README.md

# Ada Session 2 Demo

A minimal document Q&A assistant used to practise Git.

main.py

def main() -> None:
    print("Ada demo is running.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it.

macOS/Linux:

python3 main.py

Windows:

python main.py

Expected output:

Ada demo is running.

The program is intentionally tiny.

The goal is to have a runnable starting point, not a finished AI application.

22. Check Git's view of the project

Run:

git status

You should see the new files as untracked.

For example:

Untracked files:
  README.md
  main.py

What does "untracked" mean?

Git can see the files, but Git is not yet recording their history.

The files exist normally on your computer.

They simply have not been added to the next Git commit.

23. Stage the files

Run:

git add README.md main.py

Then:

git status

The files should now appear under:

Changes to be committed

What does git add do?

It puts the changes into the staging area.

It does not create a commit.

It does not upload anything to GitHub.

Think:

git add = "Include these changes in my next commit."

24. Create the first commit

Run:

git commit -m "Add runnable project scaffold"

The -m supplies the commit message.

Then:

git status

You should see:

nothing to commit, working tree clean

You have now created the first recorded state of the project.

Method 1. Stage and commit

  1. git status — see what has changed.

  2. git add <files> — stage the changes you want in this commit (git add -A stages everything).

  3. git commit -m "<message>" — record the staged changes as one commit, with a message saying what changed.

25. Meaningful commit messages

A commit message should explain what the commit changed.

Good:

Add runnable project scaffold
Clarify project objective
Document how to run the demo

Weak:

update
changes
stuff
fix
final

Useful rule

Write the message as if the sentence were:

"This commit will...".

For example:

"This commit will Add runnable project scaffold."

Say what changed. and if it's not obvious, why. Remember that (realistically) the message is the only part written for humans (and agents! we'll see).

One meaningful change per commit

A useful commit should represent a coherent change.

If you changed:

  • the prompt;
  • the README;
  • an unrelated Python function;

you may have several different changes that should not necessarily be one commit.

A useful test:

If your commit message needs several unrelated "and"s, consider splitting the work.

26. git diff

Modify README.md.

For example, change:

A minimal document Q&A assistant used to practise Git.

to:

A minimal document Q&A assistant used to practise reproducible AI development.

Run:

git status

Then:

git diff

You should see a diff similar to:

-A minimal document Q&A assistant used to practise Git.
+A minimal document Q&A assistant used to practise reproducible AI development.

What does git diff do?

It shows exactly how your files have changed.

  • - means a line was removed.
  • + means a line was added.

Use it before staging when you want to check that your change is what you intended. This is VERY useful if you code with AI :)

27. Commit the change

Run:

git add README.md
git commit -m "Clarify project objective"

Then:

git status

Your working tree should be clean.

28. git log

To see your history:

git log --oneline

You might see:

abc1234 Clarify project objective
def5678 Add runnable project scaffold

The hashes will be different on your computer. The important part is that Git now has an ordered history.

You can think of it as:

Add runnable project scaffold
          ↓
Clarify project objective

29. Committing as a reflex

Do not think:

"I need to finish the entire project before I commit."

Instead:

Meaningful change
      ↓
Check it
      ↓
Commit it
      ↓
Continue

I recommend committing often, after changes small enough to describe in one line.

Grading Standard: Consistent Evolution

The project's Git history should show how the project evolved. That means the repository should not suddenly appear fully completed at the end of the course.

30. Create a GitHub repository

Go to: https://github.com/

Create a new repository.

For the first push, create an empty repository.

Do not initialise it with:

  • README
  • .gitignore
  • license

Why?

Because we already have a local Git repository with its own history.

Starting with an empty remote keeps the first push simple.

For example, call it:

ada-session2-demo

Do not confuse:

local repository

with:

GitHub repository

At this point they are still separate.

31. Connect the local repository to GitHub

Inside your local project directory:

git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/ada-session2-demo.git

Replace the URL with your actual repository URL.

Check:

git remote -v

You should see origin.

What is origin?

origin is the conventional name for the main remote repository. It is just a nickname. You could technically call a remote something else, but origin is the standard convention.

32. Push your history to GitHub

Run:

git push -u origin main

This sends the commits from your local main branch to GitHub.

The -u establishes the upstream relationship between:

local main

and:

origin/main

The -u creates a permanent connection between your local machine and your GitHub repository.

By running this command, you are explicitly linking your local main branch to the main branch on GitHub (your origin). It builds the exact track your project will follow.

After this, future pushes can normally be:

git push

33. Commit vs push

This distinction is fundamental.

Suppose you run:

git commit -m "Record session 2 checkpoint"

but do not run:

git push

Your commit exists locally.

Your teammates do not see it on GitHub.

Now run:

git push

The committed change is sent to GitHub.

Therefore:

git commit
    ↓
records locally

git push
    ↓
sends commits to the remote

Remember:

Commit records. Push shares.

39. Simplified route if you are stuck

If the project itself is blocking you, stop building the actual AI functionality.

Use:

print("Project starts successfully.")

The goal today is Git.

If GitHub authentication is blocking you, first complete the local sequence:

git init
    ↓
git status
    ↓
git add
    ↓
git commit
    ↓
git log

Then solve the GitHub connection separately.

Do not let a login problem prevent you from learning local Git.

40. Common errors

Changes not staged for commit or nothing to commit

You executed git commit before selecting your files with git add.

Your exceptional work is safe in your working directory, but Git needs you to frame the shot before taking the picture.

The Fix:

  1. Run git status to see your modified files.
  2. Run git add <file> to stage them.
  3. Run git commit -m "..." to record the historical snapshot.

git: command not found

Git is not installed or is not available in your PATH.

Install Git and restart your terminal.

gh: command not found

GitHub CLI is not installed or is not available in your PATH.

Install gh and restart your terminal.

fatal: not a git repository

You are probably in the wrong folder.

Check:

pwd

Then navigate to your project folder.

Author identity unknown

Configure:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"

Then commit again.

remote origin already exists

Check:

git remote -v

If the URL is wrong:

git remote set-url origin <CORRECT-URL>

src refspec main does not match any

You probably have not created a commit yet.

Check:

git log --oneline

Create the first commit and then push.

GitHub says the push was rejected because histories differ

You probably created the GitHub repository with a README or another
initial file.

For this beginner workflow, the easiest solution is usually to create a
new empty GitHub repository.

Python is not recognised

Try:

python3 --version

on macOS/Linux, or:

python --version

or:

py --version

on Windows.

41. Essential commands from this session

Command Purpose

git --version Check Git installation
git init -b main Create a Git repository
git config --global user.name "..." Configure Git identity
git config --global user.email "..." Configure Git identity
git status See the current repository state
git add <file> Stage a file
git add . Stage changes in the current directory
git commit -m "..." Record a commit
git diff See unstaged changes
git log --oneline See commit history
git remote -v See configured remotes
git remote add origin <url> Add a remote
git push -u origin main Push main and set upstream
git push Push later commits
gh --version Check GitHub CLI
gh auth login Authenticate GitHub CLI
gh auth status Check GitHub authentication

42. Mental model to remember

The most important workflow from Session 2 is:

                    EDIT
                     │
                     ▼
              Working directory
                     │
                     │ git diff
                     │
                     │ git add
                     ▼
                Staging area
                     │
                     │ git commit
                     ▼
              Local Git history
                     │
                     │ git push
                     ▼
             GitHub remote

And the corresponding questions are:

What changed?
    → git diff

What state am I in?
    → git status

What should go into the next snapshot?
    → git add

Record the snapshot.
    → git commit

What happened previously?
    → git log

Share my commits.
    → git push

43. Exam-oriented concepts

You should be able to explain:

Version control

A system that records a project's history as an ordered series of states and allows you to restore, compare and reconcile changes.

Repository

A project folder together with its Git history.

Commit

A recorded state/snapshot of the project.

History

The ordered sequence of commits.

Staging area

The set of changes selected for the next commit.

Git

The version-control system.

GitHub

An online service for hosting Git repositories and supporting collaboration.

Commit vs push

A commit records changes locally.

A push sends committed changes to a remote repository.

45. Answers

1. Does git init create a GitHub repository?

No.

It creates a local Git repository.

2. Does git add create a commit?

No.

It stages changes for the next commit.

3. Does git commit upload your code?

No.

It records a snapshot locally.

4. What does git status tell you?

It tells you the current state of the repository, including branch, untracked files, staged changes and other changes.

5. What does git diff show?

It shows the line-by-line differences in your files.

6. Why have a staging area?

It lets you choose which changes belong in the next commit.

7. Git vs GitHub?

Git is the version-control system.

GitHub is an online service that hosts Git repositories and supports collaboration.

8. What does git push do?

It sends committed changes from your local repository to a remote repository.

9. What is a commit?

A recorded snapshot/state of the project.

10. Why small, meaningful commits?

They make the history easier to understand, inspect, revert and collaborate on.

46. Session 2 final checklist

Before finishing Session 2, verify:

  • Git is installed.
  • GitHub account exists.
  • GitHub email is verified.
  • gh is installed.
  • gh auth status works.
  • Python 3 is installed if needed for the starter project.
  • Terminal works.
  • Editor works.
  • The project exists locally.
  • Git has been initialised.
  • The project has at least one runnable state.
  • The first commit has been created.
  • The commit message describes the change.
  • The local repository has a clean working tree.
  • A GitHub remote has been configured.
  • The commit has been pushed to GitHub.
  • The team can see the repository on GitHub.
  • You understand commit vs push.
  • You understand working directory → staging area →
    repository.
